headline: High-risk shared-bus voice framework plus browser-capable support agent creates dangerous default pathways for leakage, injection, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can run browsers and parse files/AGENTS.md, while agent B uses a shared bus and ingests text/conversation state. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled content from A can reach B as instructions. No direct provenance controls are documented for either agent, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent A forwards browser-derived text into the shared bus used by agent B
IF agent B treats shared-bus text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding from A to B
Add a provenance tag to all bus messages
Require B to ignore untrusted markdown/instructions
Use a manual review step before B acts on A output
requires-engineering: isolate the agents onto separate buses

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches provider auth data, session history, and project code; agent B processes text, audio/video, and conversation state over a shared bus. If A’s outputs or context are placed on that bus, B can relay sensitive material through allowlisted network egress to third parties. The profiles do not show isolation or redaction by default.
conditions: IF agent A writes session history or auth prompts onto the shared bus
IF agent B sends bus contents to external STT/LLM/TTS services
mitigations: Redact secrets before any bus handoff
Turn off external service connectors in B
Keep A’s auth prompts out of shared state
Restrict bus messages to non-sensitive summaries
requires-engineering: encrypt or segregate shared state per agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network egress, browser execution, subprocesses, and file access; B has allowlisted egress and a shared bus. Their overlapping ability to mutate shared conversation state and call external services creates coordination conflicts, though the profiles do not prove same-directory filesystem writes or shared git state. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same mutable bus-backed state
IF either agent is configured to modify shared files or git state
mitigations: Assign one agent as the sole writer
Freeze shared state during critical steps
Separate external API credentials per agent
Disable concurrent edits to the same workspace
requires-engineering: add locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate browser-derived content and support artifacts, and B exposes text/conversation pipelines that may act on upstream input. If B consumes A’s output without verification, errors or hallucinations from A can cascade into downstream speech or API actions. The profiles show no built-in validation step, so the default pathway is dangerous.
conditions: IF B uses A’s output as authoritative input
IF B triggers downstream actions from unverified text
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B acts
Require citations for any factual claims from A
Limit B to read-only summarization of A output
Log and review all cross-agent handoffs
requires-engineering: add schema validation for A-to-B messages

E_compliance.rationale: A handles provider auth prompts, installation identifiers, session history, and project code; B handles conversation state, audio/video/images, and analytics/metrics. If regulated or personal data is routed from A into B’s cloud-connected services, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so the mismatch is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF personal or regulated data from A is forwarded into B’s external services
IF retention or residency policies differ between A’s and B’s providers
mitigations: Classify data before any transfer
Block regulated data from B’s external APIs
Document retention settings for both agents
Keep auth prompts out of logs
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
